text.p: One of business travel's rewards for rolling up thousands of miles in an airline's frequent flier programme is early boarding -- and first crack at the usually crowded overhead storage bins.
But sometimes that may not be worth much either.

On a recent 6:15 a.m. United Airlines flight from Chicago's O'Hare International Airport to Washington's National, the desk agent offered the usual pre-boarding for first class and "premier" passengers, the tag United gives those who travel at least 25,000 miles a year with it.
But she was quick to add "there are over 100 of you this morning," a big chunk of the passenger load.
The incident was unusual. United spokesman Joe Hopkins noted that it was the first day of the week and the first flight on a very busy route.

But he said United's programme continues to grow at all levels and now has about 25 million people enrolled. Only actual air miles travelled -- not those earned for hotel stays and the like -- are counted for preferred status.

The continued popularity of such programmes is reflected in a new survey from Reed Travel Group which found that the average U.S. traveller belongs to five mileage programmes, with 99 percent of American travelers belonging to at least one.
The airlines do not disclose actual membership in the preferred levels of such programmes, but Hopkins said those parts of its programme were also growing.

The survey from Reed, which covered more than 5,200 business travelers from nine nations, found that recognition of frequent flier status, the kind of thing that gets a passenger to the head of the line, ranks nearly as high as earning the miles themselves among those questioned.
The survey found that the most important reason for belonging to such programmes was to gain priority on waiting lists -- to snare a seat on crowded flights.

The second most important reason cited by those surveyed was the mileage credit itself followed by the upgrade possibilities such credit brings and after that by status that wins favoured recognition, and early boarding, at the gate.
The survey also turned up some interesting quirks about business travelers:
-- Three of four prefer to read in flight and rate talking to their seatmates as the last thing they want to do.

-- The British are the most likely to drink on long-haul flights, the French least likely to pay attention to safety instructions, the Germans most likely to hand over frequent flier benefits to their employers and the Italians most paranoid about being stranded without a grooming bag and a change of clothes.
-- One in four is likely to bring a laptop computer on the flight but those who do are more likely to use it in the hotel room than in the air.
-- The average business traveller makes 21 trips a year, spending 37 nights out of town.
